final_recommendation: The room converged on a negotiated settlement path contingent on three interlocking conditions: (1) FINMA issuing a factual statement distinguishing Credit Suisse's trigger as operationally broader (not drafting-defective), (2) bondholder group settling at 60 cents with full adviser release, and (3) D&O carriers committing in writing to 30-cent tail closure by end-2025. Without all three, litigation momentum remains the fallback.
minority_objections: bondholder_counsel initially rejected adviser release as validating FINMA's legal theory and creating precedent exposure
institutional_investor threatened market exit if boilerplate analysis showed industry-standard language rather than Credit Suisse outlier
key_conflicts: Adviser release requirement: bondholder_counsel saw it as precedent trap; FINMA and insurers saw it as mandatory to close reinsurer tail
Public statement on trigger language: bondholder_group demanded FINMA distinguish CS as outlier; FINMA refused to characterize competitor boilerplate as defective
Two-bite exposure: splitting FINMA settlement from D&O claims created reinsurer accumulation fears that threatened to collapse both tracks
key_concessions: FINMA agreed to factual execution-distinction statement (CS capital position crossed trigger faster) rather than drafting-defect characterization
bondholder_group accepted 60-cent recovery (down from initial 65-cent anchor) contingent on adviser release and FINMA statement
institutional_investor committed to stay in AT1 market if boilerplate analysis confirmed CS outlier status
red_lines: bondholder_counsel: no settlement validating FINMA's legal theory of trigger lawfulness in writing
institutional_investor: no capital commitment if trigger language proves market-standard across Deutsche/Barclays
insurance_observer: no reinsurer commitment without unified cross-claim release and tail closure by end-2025
FINMA: no public statement characterizing competitor AT1 boilerplate as defective or misread
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Reinsurer commitment enforceability: room assumed preliminary carrier signals would convert to binding reinsurer commitments without addressing reinsurance treaty language or capacity constraints
Execution timeline fragility: entire settlement structure depended on Friday deadline without contingency for carrier stall tactics or reinsurer pushback
Precedent contagion beyond AT1: no discussion of how settlement terms might affect CoCo bonds, Tier 2 capital, or other contingent instruments
Cross-border enforcement: dual-jurisdiction filing strategy mentioned early but settlement enforceability across US/EU/Swiss courts never developed
downstream_risk_variables: AT1 issuance costs and volumes post-settlement
Litigation against other bank advisers if CS settlement creates template
Regulatory treatment of viability triggers in future bank resolutions
Market repricing of Deutsche/Barclays AT1 based on boilerplate comparison
D&O premium inflation for bank boards and audit committees
uncertainty_notes: Three critical dependencies remained unresolved at close: (1) whether reinsurers would commit in writing to 30-cent tail closure by Friday, (2) whether FINMA's execution-distinction statement would satisfy both bondholder demands and avoid validating competitor claims, and (3) whether boilerplate analysis definitively proved CS outlier status or revealed industry-wide trigger ambiguity. Failure on any dimension collapses settlement path and reverts to litigation.

marker_evidence.litigation_likelihood: Litigation was the room's constant fallback and leverage anchor—dual-jurisdiction filing approved R1, D&O claims filed R3, settlement negotiations explicitly framed as litigation-avoidance with Friday deadlines driving every concession.
marker_evidence.regulatory_legitimacy_challenge: FINMA's trigger interpretation and weekend ordinance authority were contested throughout (bondholder_counsel called joint statement a 'settlement trap'), but the room ultimately accepted execution-distinction framing rather than pursuing full legal invalidation.
marker_evidence.creditor_hierarchy_controversy: Equity-over-AT1 inversion mentioned only in passing as 'hierarchy_precedent_damage' variable; never developed as a substantive legal or negotiating argument—room focused on trigger language and settlement mechanics instead.
marker_evidence.market_confidence_damage: AT1 repricing risk and contagion to Deutsche/Barclays drove multiple decision points (boilerplate analysis publication, institutional_investor's 60-cent conditionality), but was secondary to litigation/settlement mechanics as the room's organizing logic.
marker_evidence.claims_tail: Multi-year, multi-party claims exposure dominated the entire arc—two-bite reinsurer fears, 2026 tail closure, fragmented discovery across jurisdictions, and insurer capacity constraints were the central obstacles to settlement from R3 onward.
marker_evidence.financial_lines_relevance: D&O/E&O exposure was a primary driver from R3 forward—separate adviser claims filed, reinsurer commitment requirements, 30-cent cap negotiations, and tail-closure deadlines structured the entire settlement path and were explicitly named as deal-breakers.
